```{r setup}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| paged-print: false

library(janitor)
library(car)                # Anova()
library(MASS)               # glm.nb()
library(performance)        # check_overdispersion(), check_model(), r2()
library(DHARMa)             # simulateResiduals()
library(emmeans)
library(broom)
library(parameters)         # model_parameters()
library(pscl)               # pR2()
library(ResourceSelection)  # hoslem.test()
library(patchwork)
library(tidyverse)

options(scipen = 999)

# ---- Galapagos plant richness - Gotelli & Ellison, the SAME file used in
#      week 6 (correlation & linear models). 17 islands, corrected areas. ----
g_df <- read_csv("data/galapagos_species_area.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# ---- Gotelli & Ellison New England ant species density - the count where
#      the Poisson actually fits ----
ant_df <- read_csv("data/gotelli_ant_species.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# ---- Sargent & Lodge crayfish - last week's data, used in Part 8 to show
#      that a one-way ANOVA IS a Gaussian GLM ----
cray_df <- read_csv("data/sargent_lodge_crayfish.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  clean_names() %>%
  mutate(range = factor(range, levels = c("Native", "Invasive")))

# ---- Polis et al. (1998) Uta lizards - Quinn & Keough Box 13-1 ----
polis_df <- read_csv("data/polis.csv", na = c(".", ""),
                     show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  clean_names() %>%
  drop_na(paratio, pa)

# ---- Bolger et al. (1997) canyon rodents - Quinn & Keough Box 13-2 ----
bolger_df <- read_csv("data/bolger.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  clean_names()
```

## Part 1 · Why the Linear Model Runs Out {.divider}

## Where We Left Off

:::::: columns
:::: {.column width="55%"}
Three weeks of **linear models**:

-   One-way ANOVA
-   Factorial ANOVA I
-   Factorial ANOVA II — the redux

Every one of them assumed:

-   **Normality** of the residuals
-   **Homogeneity of variance** — Levene's or Breusch–Pagan
-   **Independence** of observations
::::

:::: {.column width="45%"}
::: callout-important
**Those assumptions are about the residuals, not the raw data** — but when the response is a *count* or a *yes/no*, they fail in a way no transformation fully repairs.

Today: keep the linear part, change the distribution.
:::
::::
::::::

## The Data: Galápagos Island Biogeography

::::: columns
::: {.column width="54%"}
Gotelli & Ellison's Galápagos data — **17 islands**, plant species
richness against island area.

| Column | What it is |
|-------------|------------------------------------|
| `island` | island name (the historical names) |
| `area_km2` | island area, km² |
| `n_species` | number of plant species — **a count** |

::: callout-tip
**You have already analysed this dataset.** In **week 6** you fitted
$\log_{10}(S) \sim \log_{10}(A)$ to it and used it for the
influential-point demonstration.

Same islands, same question. Today the response gets treated as what it
actually is — a **count**.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="46%"}
```{r glm-01}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| fig-width: 3.6
#| fig-alt: "Histogram of plant species counts across the 17 Galapagos islands, strongly right-skewed with most islands under 100 species and a long tail out past 300."

ggplot(g_df, aes(x = n_species)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 25, fill = "darkblue", color = "white") +
  labs(x = "Number of plant species", y = "Number of islands") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10)
```

```{r glm-02}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
g_df %>%
  summarise(n = n(),
            min = min(n_species),
            max = max(n_species))
```
:::
:::::

## A Count Is Not a Normal Variable {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
A count has three properties a normal distribution does not:

1.  It is a **whole number**
2.  It **cannot go below zero**
3.  Its **variance grows with its mean**

```{r glm-03}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
g_df %>%
  summarise(mean_spp = mean(n_species),
            var_spp  = var(n_species),
            ratio    = var_spp / mean_spp)
```

The variance is **103×** the mean. A normal distribution is free to have
any variance it likes, so that ratio is not itself a violation — but
hold on to it. The Poisson will insist it is **1**.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r glm-04}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-width: 3.6
#| fig-alt: "Scatterplot of plant species against island area in square kilometres on the raw scale, showing almost all islands crushed against the left axis and one very large island far to the right."

ggplot(g_df, aes(x = area_km2, y = n_species)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Island area (km²)", y = "Number of plant species") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10)
```

::: callout-warning
**On the raw scale the relationship is unreadable** — area spans four
orders of magnitude. Both axes need logs, which is exactly what you did
in week 6.
:::
:::
:::::

## Fit Last Week's Model Anyway — and Watch It Fail {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r glm-05}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
lm_raw <- lm(n_species ~ area_km2, data = g_df)

glance(lm_raw) %>%
  dplyr::select(r.squared, p.value)
```

```{r glm-06}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
shapiro.test(residuals(lm_raw))$p.value

# predict the SMALLEST island
predict(lm_raw,
        newdata = data.frame(area_km2 = 0.518),
        interval = "prediction")
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: callout-important
**The model predicts a 95% interval of −111 to 302 species.**

A negative number of plant species is not a wide interval. It is an
**impossible** one.
:::

-   Normality of residuals: ***p* = 0.002** — it fails
-   Equal variance: Breusch–Pagan *p* = 0.66 — this one is **fine**

The question is not wrong. Area almost certainly does drive richness.
The *model being used to answer it* is making promises the data cannot
keep — chiefly that the response is free to go negative.

**Say only what the diagnostics say.** Here variance is not the problem;
the normal distribution's unbounded support is.
:::
:::::

## You Already Know One Fix — You Used It in Week 6 {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r glm-06b}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
lm_log <- lm(log10(n_species) ~ log10(area_km2),
             data = g_df)

glance(lm_log) %>%
  dplyr::select(r.squared, p.value)

shapiro.test(residuals(lm_log))$p.value
```

R² rises from 0.33 to **0.59**, normality goes from *p* = 0.002 to
***p* = 0.48**, and the slope **0.331** is the species–area exponent *z*.

**The transformation works.** So why is there anything left to teach?
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
Three reasons, and each one is a thing a GLM does that a transformation
cannot.

1.  **A count is discrete.** The log of a count is a continuous variable
    that the data can never actually take.

2.  **`log(0)` is undefined.** No island here has zero species, but an
    island with none is a real observation — and then the transformation
    needs a fudge (`log(y + 1)`) that changes the answer.

3.  **It answers a different question.** `lm` on logged counts models
    the mean of the log, which back-transforms to the **geometric**
    mean.

```{r glm-06c}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
c(arithmetic = mean(g_df$n_species),
  geometric  = exp(mean(log(g_df$n_species))))
```

**119.3 versus 73.6 species.** Two different quantities — and the
transformation silently hands you the second one.
:::
:::::

## What a GLM Changes

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
A **generalized linear model** keeps the linear part — $\beta_0 +
\beta_1 X_1 + \dots$ — and swaps out two things.

| Component | What it is | Example |
|------------------|------------------------|---------------|
| **Random** | the response's distribution | Poisson for counts |
| **Systematic** | the predictors | `log(area_km2)` |
| **Link** | connects the mean to the predictors | `log` for counts |

$$g(\mu) = \beta_0 + \beta_1X_1 + \beta_2X_2 \dots$$

GLMs are fitted by **maximum likelihood** (ML), not ordinary least
squares (OLS) — which is why their output talks about *deviance* rather
than sums of squares.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
```{r glm-07}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-width: 3.4
#| fig-alt: "Three example distributions from the exponential family: a normal density curve on top, and a Poisson (lambda = 3) and a binomial (n = 10, p = 0.3) bar distribution side by side below."

x <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 100)

p1 <- ggplot(data.frame(x, d = dnorm(x)), aes(x, d)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(title = "Normal", x = "Value", y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 7)

p2 <- ggplot(data.frame(x = 0:10, y = dpois(0:10, 3)), aes(x, y)) +
  geom_col(fill = "darkblue") +
  labs(title = "Poisson (λ = 3)", x = "Count", y = "Prob.") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 7)

p3 <- ggplot(data.frame(x = 0:10, y = dbinom(0:10, 10, 0.3)), aes(x, y)) +
  geom_col(fill = "darkred") +
  labs(title = "Binomial (n = 10, p = 0.3)", x = "Successes", y = "Prob.") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 7)

(p1 / (p2 + p3))
```
:::
:::::

## Choosing the Family and the Link

::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
### What the response looks like

| Response | Family |
|-------------------------------|-------------------------|
| continuous, symmetric | `gaussian` — this is `lm()` |
| counts | `poisson` |
| counts, variance > mean | negative binomial (`glm.nb`) |
| binary — present/absent | `binomial(link = "logit")` |
| positive, continuous, skewed | `Gamma` |
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
### The link function

| Distribution | Link | Formula |
|--------------|----------|------------------------------|
| Normal | Identity | $g(\mu) = \mu$ |
| Poisson | Log | $g(\mu) = \log(\mu)$ |
| Binomial | Logit | $g(\mu) = \log[\mu/(1-\mu)]$ |
| Gamma | Log | $g(\mu) = \log(\mu)$ |

::: callout-tip
**The link is what keeps predictions possible.** A `log` link cannot
predict a negative count. A `logit` link cannot predict a probability
above 1.
:::
:::
:::::

## Part 2 · Gaussian GLMs — the Sanity Check {.divider}

## Before Trusting `glm()`, Check It Against What You Know

Before handing `glm()` an unfamiliar distribution, confirm it reproduces
the model you already trust.

A **Gaussian** family with an **identity** link *is* a linear model —
same estimates, same standard errors, same *p*-values. If that does not
come out identical, you have mis-specified something.

::: callout-note
**You are not learning a new model.** You are learning two arguments on
the one you already have: `family =` and `link =`. Everything that
follows today changes exactly those two.
:::

## Gaussian GLM — Same Model, Two Function Calls {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r glm-08}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
lm_model <- lm(n_species ~ log(area_km2),
               data = g_df)

gauss_model <- glm(n_species ~ log(area_km2),
                   data = g_df,
                   family = gaussian(link = "identity"))

round(cbind(lm  = coef(lm_model),
            glm = coef(gauss_model)), 6)
```

```{r glm-09}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
all.equal(coef(lm_model), coef(gauss_model))
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r glm-10}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
Anova(gauss_model, type = "III", test = "F")
```

Identical to `Anova()` on the `lm` — identical estimates, identical
*F*, and identical for the same reason: it **is** that model, fitted by
a different algorithm.
:::
:::::

## Gaussian GLM — Reading the New Vocabulary {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="48%"}
```{r glm-11}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
data.frame(
  `GLM summary says` = c("Dispersion parameter",
                         "Null deviance",
                         "Residual deviance",
                         "null - residual"),
  value = round(c(summary(gauss_model)$dispersion,
                  gauss_model$null.deviance,
                  gauss_model$deviance,
                  gauss_model$null.deviance - gauss_model$deviance), 1),
  `ANOVA calls it` = c("Residual mean square",
                       "SS total",
                       "SS residual",
                       "SS log(area)"),
  check.names = FALSE)
```
:::

::: {.column width="52%"}
A GLM summary renames three things you already know:

-   **Dispersion parameter** — for a Gaussian GLM this is the
    **residual variance**, $\sigma^2$. It is the ANOVA table's residual
    mean square.

-   **Null deviance** — the error left when you predict every island
    with the **grand mean** alone. For a Gaussian GLM this is
    **SS~total~**.

-   **Residual deviance** — the error left **after** fitting the
    predictor. For a Gaussian GLM this is **SS~residual~**.

::: callout-important
Null deviance − residual deviance = the **model** sum of squares. The
residual deviance is the part your predictor did *not* explain.
:::
:::
:::::

## Part 3 · Poisson GLMs for Count Data {.divider}

## The Poisson Distribution and Its One Strong Claim

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
**Poisson** is *the* distribution for counts:

-   Number of species on an island
-   Number of parasites in a host
-   Number of nests in a plot

It assumes:

-   Counts are non-negative integers
-   Events occur **independently**
-   **The mean equals the variance**

That third one is not a convenience. Poisson has only **one** parameter,
λ, which is simultaneously its mean and its variance. You do not get to
set them separately.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: callout-warning
**Remember the ratio.** The variance of `n_species` is **103×** its
mean.

Poisson insists that ratio is **1**.

Fit it anyway — the failure is the content.
:::

::: callout-tip
**Why `log` is the link.** $\log(\mu)$ runs from −∞ to +∞, so the linear
predictor can be any number at all and $\mu = e^{\eta}$ is still
positive. Counts can never come out negative.
:::
:::
:::::

## Fitting the Poisson GLM {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r glm-12}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
poiss_model <- glm(n_species ~ log(area_km2),
                   data = g_df,
                   family = poisson(link = "log"))

round(summary(poiss_model)$coefficients, 4)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
The model predicts the **natural log** of the expected count, so
exponentiate to read it:

-   Slope **0.2875** on the log scale
-   $e^{0.2875} = 1.333$ — every **e-fold** (2.72×) increase in area
    multiplies expected richness by **1.33**
-   Equivalently, a **doubling** of area multiplies richness by
    $2^{0.2875} = 1.22$ — a 22% gain

::: callout-important
With a log link, coefficients are **multiplicative**, not additive. A
coefficient of β multiplies the mean by $e^{\beta}$.
:::

Compare that 0.2875 with week 6's log–log slope of **0.331**. Close, but
**not the same number** — and the next slide but one says why.
:::
:::::

## Testing the Effect — Why LR and Not *F* {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r glm-13}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
Anova(poiss_model, type = "III", test = "LR")
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
-   An ANOVA *F*-test is a **ratio of variances**, and its denominator
    is the residual mean square — an estimate of $\sigma^2$.

-   A Poisson GLM **never estimates a $\sigma^2$**. The variance is not
    a free parameter; it is pinned to the mean. There is nothing to put
    in the denominator.

-   So we use a **likelihood ratio (LR)** test instead: fit the model
    with the predictor and the model without it, and compare how much
    better the full model explains the data.

$$\text{LR } \chi^2 = 2(\log L_{full} - \log L_{reduced})$$

**Hold on to that χ² of 979.** It is about to shrink to 24.
:::
:::::

## Three Ways to Say "Log" — and Why They Differ

::: {.compact-table}
| Model | R code | Interpretation of β₁ |
|--------------|------------------------|---------------------------------|
| **GLM, log link** | `glm(Y ~ X, family = poisson)` | A 1-unit change in X multiplies the **mean** of Y by $e^{\beta_1}$ |
| **lm on logged Y** | `lm(log(Y) ~ X)` | A 1-unit change in X multiplies the **median** of Y by $e^{\beta_1}$ |
| **log-log** | `lm(log(Y) ~ log(X))` | A 1% change in X gives a β₁% change in Y — **week 6** |
:::

::: callout-important
**These are not the same model.** A GLM with a log link models the log
of the mean, $\log(E[Y])$. Logging the response models the mean of the
log, $E[\log(Y)]$ — which back-transforms to a **geometric** mean, not
an arithmetic one: **73.6 species, not 119.3**. The GLM also never has
to decide what to do with a zero count.
:::

That is the whole difference between **0.2875** and **0.331**. Neither
is a mistake; they are answers to two different questions.

## Part 4 · Overdispersion and the Negative Binomial {.divider}

## Checking Dispersion — the Test That Matters {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
The **dispersion parameter** is observed variance over expected
variance:

$$\hat\phi = \frac{\sum \text{(Pearson residual)}^2}{\text{residual df}}$$

-   **≈ 1** — good fit, variance = mean
-   **> 1** — **overdispersion**, variance > mean
-   **< 1** — underdispersion

```{r glm-14}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
check_overdispersion(poiss_model)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: callout-warning
**Dispersion ratio 39.7, not 1.**

The model claims the variance in richness on the largest island is equal
to its mean — about 325. The data say it is far larger.
:::

> ⚠️ `shapiro.test(residuals(poiss_model))` will **run**, and give you a
> number. The number is meaningless — normality of raw residuals is not
> a Poisson assumption.
>
> **R will not stop you running a test that does not apply.** Check the
> diagnostic that matches the model, not the one you remember.
:::
:::::

## The DHARMa Residual Check

::: {.panel column="screen"}
```{r glm-15}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-alt: "DHARMa diagnostic plots for the Poisson GLM: a QQ-plot of scaled residuals showing severe departure with significant KS, dispersion and outlier tests, and a scaled-residuals-versus-predicted plot with significant quantile deviations."

set.seed(123)
sim_poiss <- simulateResiduals(poiss_model, n = 1000)
plot(sim_poiss)
```
:::

Ordinary GLM residuals are hard to read. **DHARMa** simulates from the
fitted model and asks where each observation falls in its own predicted
distribution — if the model is right, those are uniform. Here they are
not, and the problem is not subtle.

## The Negative Binomial — a Second Parameter {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
The negative binomial adds **theta** (θ), which lets the variance exceed
the mean by as much as it needs to:

$$\operatorname{Var}(Y) = \mu + \frac{\mu^2}{\theta}$$

As θ → ∞ this collapses back to the Poisson. A **small** θ means a lot
of extra spread.

```{r glm-16}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
nb_model <- glm.nb(n_species ~ log(area_km2),
                   data = g_df)

c(theta = nb_model$theta)

check_overdispersion(nb_model)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r glm-17}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
Anova(nb_model, type = "III", test = "LR")

AIC(poiss_model, nb_model)
```

::: callout-note
The dispersion is gone — 39.7 down to **0.68** — and the AIC drops by
**496**. Same data, same predictor, same link. The only thing added was
permission for the variance to be larger than the mean.
:::
:::
:::::

## What Overdispersion Did to Your *p*-Value {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r glm-18}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
cbind(estimate = round(coef(poiss_model), 4),
      SE_poisson = round(summary(poiss_model)$coefficients[, 2], 4),
      SE_negbin  = round(summary(nb_model)$coefficients[, 2], 4))
```

::: {.compact-table}
| | Poisson | Negative binomial |
|------------------------|------------|------------------|
| slope | 0.2875 | 0.2988 |
| **SE of the slope** | **0.0096** | **0.0610** |
| LR χ² | **979** | **23.8** |
| dispersion ratio | 39.7 | 0.68 |
| AIC | 682.8 | 187.0 |
:::
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: callout-important
**The slope barely moved — 0.2875 to 0.2988. The standard error moved
6.4-fold.**

The two models put the line in essentially the same place. What changed
is how certain they claim to be about it.
:::

Overdispersion does not move your estimate. It makes you **far more
confident in it than you are entitled to be** — smaller SEs, bigger test
statistics, narrower intervals, smaller *p*-values.

`summary(poiss_model)` reports *p* ≈ 10⁻¹⁹⁸ for this slope. That is not a
result; it is an arithmetic consequence of an assumption nobody checked.

Both models here still say *p* < 0.001. The conclusion did not change.
Only the **honesty** of it did — and your homework is the dataset where
it very nearly flips.
:::
:::::

## Not Every Count Is Overdispersed {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
Gotelli & Ellison's New England **ant species density** — 22 bogs, ant
richness against latitude and elevation.

```{r glm-18b}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
ant_df %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(n_ant_species),
            var  = var(n_ant_species),
            ratio = var / mean)
```

The raw variance-to-mean ratio is **2.02**. On the Galápagos logic, that
looks like trouble.

```{r glm-18c}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
ant_poiss <- glm(n_ant_species ~ latitude + elevation_m,
                 data = ant_df,
                 family = poisson(link = "log"))

check_overdispersion(ant_poiss)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: callout-important
**Dispersion 0.83, *p* = 0.68. The Poisson is the right model here.**

Fit the negative binomial anyway and θ comes back at about **184,000** —
`glm.nb` is telling you it found no extra variance to absorb — and the
AIC gets *worse*, 109.6 → 111.6.
:::

**Overdispersion is a property of the model, not of the data.** The raw
ratio of 2.02 was variation *between* bogs at different latitudes and
elevations. Once the predictors account for it, nothing is left over.

::: callout-tip
**So the lesson is not "counts need a negative binomial."** It is: fit
the Poisson, **check the dispersion**, and only reach for θ when the
check tells you to.

Ant richness falls **21% per degree of latitude** (*p* = 0.002) — a real
result, from the simpler model.
:::
:::
:::::


## Part 5 · Logistic Regression {.divider}

## A Binary Response Is the Other Kind of Non-Normal

:::::: columns
:::: {.column width="58%"}
A count was one kind of non-normal response. A **yes/no** is another —
dead/alive, present/absent, infected/healthy.

Logistic regression models the **probability** that Y = 1:

$$\pi(x) = \frac{e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 x}}{1 + e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 x}}$$

The **logit** link stretches probability — stuck between 0 and 1 — onto
a scale that runs from −∞ to +∞:

$$g(x) = \log\left(\frac{\pi(x)}{1-\pi(x)}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x$$

The thing inside the log, $\pi/(1-\pi)$, is the **odds**. So the linear
model is a model of **log-odds**.

::: callout-note
Gotelli & Ellison, *A Primer of Ecological Statistics*, Ch. 11 — The
Analysis of Categorical Data, for logistic regression and binomial GLMs.
:::
::::

::: {.column width="42%"}
```{r glm-22}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| fig-width: 3.4
#| fig-alt: "S-shaped logistic curve mapping the linear predictor to probability, with dashed reference lines at probability 0, 0.5 and 1 and at a linear predictor of 0."

sig <- data.frame(x = seq(-6, 6, length.out = 200)) %>%
  mutate(p = 1 / (1 + exp(-x)))

ggplot(sig, aes(x, p)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2, color = "darkblue") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(0, 0.5, 1), linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  labs(x = "Linear predictor (β₀ + β₁x)", y = "Probability π(x)") +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.25)) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9)
```
:::
::::::

## The Polis Lizard Data {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
Polis et al. (1998) recorded whether the lizard *Uta* was present on
**19 islands** in the Gulf of California, against each island's
**perimeter-to-area ratio** — a measure of how exposed its shoreline is.

```{r glm-23}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
polis_df %>%
  dplyr::select(island, paratio, uta, pa) %>%
  head(5)

count(polis_df, uta)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r glm-24}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| fig-width: 3.6
#| fig-alt: "Scatterplot of Uta lizard presence coded 0 or 1 against each island's perimeter-to-area ratio, with presence concentrated at low ratios and absence at high ratios."

ggplot(polis_df, aes(paratio, pa)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Perimeter / area ratio", y = "Uta present (1) / absent (0)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10)
```

::: callout-note
These are the data from the paper, as reproduced in **Quinn & Keough
Box 13-1** — the same file the activity uses.
:::
:::
:::::

## Fitting the Logistic Model {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r glm-25}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
lizard_model <- glm(pa ~ paratio,
                    data = polis_df,
                    family = binomial(link = "logit"))

round(summary(lizard_model)$coefficients, 4)
```

Two ways to test $H_0: \beta_1 = 0$:

1.  **Wald test** — estimate / SE, the `z` column above
2.  **Likelihood ratio test** — compare the full model to one with no
    predictor
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r glm-26}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
null_model <- glm(pa ~ 1, data = polis_df,
                  family = binomial(link = "logit"))

anova(null_model, lizard_model, test = "Chisq")
```

The LR test is the one to report — it is better behaved at small *n*,
and 19 islands is small.
:::
:::::

## The Fitted Probability Curve

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r glm-27}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-width: 4.4
#| fig-alt: "Observed Uta presence and absence plotted against perimeter-to-area ratio with the fitted logistic probability curve and its confidence band overlaid, falling from near 1 at low ratios to near 0 above a ratio of about 25."

pred_df <- data.frame(
  paratio = seq(min(polis_df$paratio), max(polis_df$paratio),
                length.out = 200))
pl <- predict(lizard_model, newdata = pred_df, type = "link", se.fit = TRUE)
pred_df <- pred_df %>%
  mutate(prob = plogis(pl$fit),
         lo   = plogis(pl$fit - 1.96 * pl$se.fit),
         hi   = plogis(pl$fit + 1.96 * pl$se.fit))

ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(data = pred_df, aes(paratio, ymin = lo, ymax = hi),
              fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(data = pred_df, aes(paratio, prob),
            color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(data = polis_df, aes(paratio, pa), size = 2.5, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dotted") +
  labs(x = "Perimeter / area ratio", y = "Probability Uta present") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10)
```
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
The curve crosses **p = 0.5** at a perimeter-to-area ratio of

$$-\frac{\beta_0}{\beta_1} = -\frac{3.606}{-0.2196} = 16.4$$

Below that, *Uta* is more likely present than absent; above it, more
likely absent.

::: callout-tip
**The curve is the link doing its job.** A straight line would have
crossed below zero on the right of this plot and predicted a negative
probability.
:::
:::
:::::

## Interpreting the Odds Ratio {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="48%"}
```{r glm-28}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
exp(coef(lizard_model))

exp(confint(lizard_model, "paratio"))
```
:::

::: {.column width="52%"}
**Odds ratio = $e^{\beta_1}$**

-   **> 1** — raising the predictor raises the odds
-   **< 1** — raising the predictor lowers the odds
-   **= 1** — no effect

Here the odds ratio is **0.803**:

-   One extra unit of perimeter-to-area ratio multiplies the odds of
    finding *Uta* by **0.80**
-   That is a **19.7%** drop in the odds per unit (1 − 0.803)
-   The CI is **0.616 to 0.936** — entirely below 1, so the relationship
    is negative

::: callout-important
For an odds ratio the null value is **1, not 0** — it lives on a
multiplicative scale. A CI that excludes 1 is the significant one.
:::
:::
:::::

## Assessing Model Fit {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r glm-29}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
# McFadden's, by hand
1 - lizard_model$deviance /
      lizard_model$null.deviance

r2(lizard_model)   # performance's default

hoslem.test(lizard_model$y,
            fitted(lizard_model), g = 10)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**McFadden's pseudo-R²** = $1 - \dfrac{D_{resid}}{D_{null}}$ = **0.459**.
`performance::r2()` instead reports **Tjur's R² = 0.521**.

Both are "pseudo" because there is no residual variance to partition —
the response is 0 or 1, so "proportion of variance explained" has
nothing to be a proportion *of*. They are different quantities, so
**say which one you report**. For McFadden's, treat 0.2–0.4 as a strong
model, not the 0.7 you would want from a regression.

::: callout-warning
**Hosmer–Lemeshow runs backwards.** Its null hypothesis is that the
model fits. You **want** *p* large. Here *p* = 0.44, so there is no
evidence of poor fit.

That is the opposite of every test you have run this semester — and it
is why a "non-significant" result is not always bad news.
:::
:::
:::::

## Part 6 · Multiple Logistic Regression {.divider}

## The Bolger Canyon Fragment Data {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
Logistic regression extends to several predictors exactly as regression
does:

$$g(x) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \ldots + \beta_p x_p$$

Bolger et al. (1997) recorded whether **native rodents** were present in
**25 canyon fragments** in coastal southern California, against three
predictors.

::: {.compact-table}
| Column | What it is |
|------------|--------------------------------|
| `rodentsp` | 1 = rodents present, 0 = absent |
| `pershrub` | % shrub cover |
| `distx` | distance to source canyon, m |
| `age` | years since isolation |
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r glm-30}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
rodent_model <- glm(
  rodentsp ~ distx + age + pershrub,
  data = bolger_df,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"))

round(summary(rodent_model)$coefficients, 4)
```

::: callout-note
Quinn & Keough **Box 13-2**. Two predictors measure **isolation**
(`distx`, `age`); one measures **habitat quality** (`pershrub`).
:::
:::
:::::

## Testing Each Predictor {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r glm-31}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
Anova(rodent_model, type = "II", test = "LR")
```

Each row drops **one** predictor and compares the two models by
likelihood ratio — the multi-predictor version of what we did to the
lizard model.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r glm-32}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
round(exp(cbind(OR = coef(rodent_model),
                confint(rodent_model)))[-1, ], 4)
```

::: callout-important
**Shrub cover is the only one that matters.** Each extra percentage
point of shrub cover multiplies the odds of rodent presence by **1.10**
(CI 1.03–1.22).

Neither isolation measure comes close — and both of their CIs bracket 1.
:::
:::
:::::

## Visualizing Each Effect

::: {.panel column="screen"}
```{r glm-33}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-height: 2.9
#| fig-width: 9.5
#| fig-alt: "Three side-by-side plots of the predicted probability of rodent presence against distance to source, years since isolation, and percent shrub cover, each holding the other two predictors at their means, with observed outcomes as a rug along the bottom. Only shrub cover shows a steep rise."

predict_for_var <- function(var_name, model, data) {
  pred_df <- data.frame(x = seq(min(data[[var_name]]), max(data[[var_name]]),
                                length.out = 100))
  names(pred_df) <- var_name
  for (ov in setdiff(c("distx", "age", "pershrub"), var_name)) {
    pred_df[[ov]] <- mean(data[[ov]])
  }
  pred_df$prob <- predict(model, newdata = pred_df, type = "response")
  pred_df
}

one_panel <- function(v, lab, col) {
  ggplot() +
    geom_rug(data = bolger_df, aes(x = .data[[v]]), sides = "b", alpha = 0.7) +
    geom_line(data = predict_for_var(v, rodent_model, bolger_df),
              aes(.data[[v]], prob), color = col, linewidth = 1) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
    labs(x = lab, y = "P(present)") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 9)
}

one_panel("distx", "Distance to source (m)", "darkred") +
  one_panel("age", "Years since isolation", "darkgreen") +
  one_panel("pershrub", "Shrub cover (%)", "darkblue")
```
:::

Each panel moves **one** predictor across its observed range and holds
the other two at their means. Only shrub cover takes the probability
from near 0 to near 1.

## Model Comparison and Selection {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r glm-34}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
mods <- list(
  "Full"            = rodent_model,
  "No distance"     = glm(rodentsp ~ age + pershrub, bolger_df, family = binomial),
  "No age"          = glm(rodentsp ~ distx + pershrub, bolger_df, family = binomial),
  "Shrub only"      = glm(rodentsp ~ pershrub, bolger_df, family = binomial),
  "No shrub"        = glm(rodentsp ~ distx + age, bolger_df, family = binomial),
  "Intercept only"  = glm(rodentsp ~ 1, bolger_df, family = binomial))

data.frame(Model = names(mods),
           k     = sapply(mods, \(m) length(coef(m))),
           AIC   = round(sapply(mods, AIC), 2),
           Deviance = round(sapply(mods, deviance), 2),
           row.names = NULL) %>%
  arrange(AIC)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
-   **Likelihood ratio tests** compare *nested* models — one must be a
    special case of the other
-   **AIC / BIC** compare any models fitted to the same data, nested or
    not
-   AIC rewards fit and penalises parameters: $AIC = -2\log L + 2k$

::: callout-note
Dropping `distx` or `age` **improves** the AIC — they were costing a
parameter each and buying almost nothing. Dropping `pershrub` makes it
far worse.
:::
:::
:::::

## How Well Does It Classify? {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r glm-35}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
pred_prob  <- predict(rodent_model, type = "response")
pred_class <- ifelse(pred_prob > 0.5, 1, 0)

cm <- table(Predicted = pred_class,
            Actual = bolger_df$rodentsp)
cm

round(c(accuracy    = sum(diag(cm)) / sum(cm),
        sensitivity = cm["1","1"] / sum(cm[, "1"]),
        specificity = cm["0","0"] / sum(cm[, "0"])), 3)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
-   **Accuracy** — fraction of fragments called correctly
-   **Sensitivity** — of the fragments that *had* rodents, how many did
    we catch?
-   **Specificity** — of the fragments that did *not*, how many did we
    correctly rule out?

::: callout-warning
**The 0.5 cut-off is a choice, not a result.** Move it and sensitivity
and specificity trade against each other. Classification accuracy is
also optimistic here — we are scoring the model on the same 25
fragments we fitted it to.
:::
:::
:::::

## Publication-Quality Figure

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r glm-36}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| fig-width: 4.6
#| fig-alt: "Publication-quality plot of the probability of native rodent presence against percent shrub cover, with jittered observed outcomes, a fitted logistic curve, and a shaded 95% confidence band rising from near zero below 20% cover to near one above 70%."

shrub_pred <- predict_for_var("pershrub", rodent_model, bolger_df)
ps <- predict(rodent_model, newdata = shrub_pred, type = "link", se.fit = TRUE)
shrub_pred <- shrub_pred %>%
  mutate(prob = plogis(ps$fit),
         lo   = plogis(ps$fit - 1.96 * ps$se.fit),
         hi   = plogis(ps$fit + 1.96 * ps$se.fit))

ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(data = shrub_pred, aes(pershrub, ymin = lo, ymax = hi),
              fill = "darkblue", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(data = shrub_pred, aes(pershrub, prob),
            color = "darkblue", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_jitter(data = bolger_df, aes(pershrub, rodentsp),
              width = 0, height = 0.03, alpha = 0.6, size = 2.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.25)) +
  labs(x = "Shrub cover (%)",
       y = "Probability of native rodent presence") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(axis.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
What makes this publishable rather than exploratory:

-   The **raw data** are visible under the fit, jittered just enough to
    separate ties
-   The **confidence band** is on the probability scale, computed on the
    link scale and back-transformed — so it can never leave [0, 1]
-   Axis labels name the **units**, not the column names
-   The other two predictors are held at their means, and the caption
    must say so

This is the shape of the graded figure in section 10 of the activity.
:::
:::::

## Scientific Write-Up — Results

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Results

The presence of native rodents in 25 canyon fragments was modelled by
multiple logistic regression with three predictors: distance to the
nearest source canyon, years since isolation, and percentage shrub
cover. The three predictors together improved substantially on the null
model (likelihood-ratio χ² = 15.26, df = 3, *p* = 0.002; McFadden's
R² = 0.44).

**Shrub cover was the only predictor with a detectable effect**
(β = 0.096, SE = 0.041, LR χ² = 9.56, df = 1, *p* = 0.002). Each
additional percentage point of shrub cover multiplied the odds of rodent
presence by 1.10 (95% CI 1.03–1.22). Neither distance to the source
canyon (LR χ² = 0.16, *p* = 0.69) nor years since isolation
(LR χ² = 0.44, *p* = 0.50) was distinguishable from zero.

The model classified 80% of fragments correctly (sensitivity 0.75,
specificity 0.85) and showed no evidence of lack of fit
(Hosmer–Lemeshow χ² = 6.04, df = 8, *p* = 0.64).
:::

## Scientific Write-Up — Discussion

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Discussion

Vegetation structure, not isolation, predicted whether native rodents
persisted in these canyon fragments. Shrub cover is plausibly acting as
both food and cover from predators, and the effect is large enough to
matter on the ground: holding distance and age at their means, a
fragment at 70% shrub cover has an 88% chance of retaining its rodents,
against 6% for one at 20%.

The two isolation measures showed no detectable relationship. With 25
fragments, **failing to detect an effect is not the same as showing
there is none** — but the AIC comparison points the same way, since
dropping either one improved the model. The practical reading is that
within this range of fragment ages and distances, habitat quality
dominates.
:::

## Part 7 · Diagnostics and Assumptions {.divider}

## Assumptions of Logistic Regression {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="45%"}
1.  **Independence** of observations
2.  **Linearity** between each predictor and the **log odds** — not the
    probability
3.  No extreme outliers or high-leverage points
4.  No multicollinearity among predictors
5.  Enough data per parameter — a rough rule is **10 events per
    predictor**

::: callout-warning
Assumption 2 is the one people forget. Logistic regression does **not**
assume a linear relationship with the probability — the curve is
S-shaped by construction. It assumes linearity on the **logit** scale.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r glm-37}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-height: 3.3
#| fig-width: 5.0
#| fig-alt: "Three small panels of binned empirical log-odds of rodent presence against distance, age and shrub cover, each with a straight-line fit, used to check the linearity-on-the-logit-scale assumption."

check_linearity <- function(var, lab) {
  bolger_df %>%
    mutate(bin = cut(.data[[var]], breaks = 4)) %>%
    group_by(bin) %>%
    summarise(mean_var = mean(.data[[var]]),
              p = (sum(rodentsp) + 0.5) / (n() + 1), .groups = "drop") %>%
    mutate(logodds = log(p / (1 - p))) %>%
    ggplot(aes(mean_var, logodds)) +
    geom_point(size = 2.5) +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "red", linewidth = 0.7) +
    labs(x = lab, y = "Log odds") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 8)
}

check_linearity("distx", "Distance (m)") +
  check_linearity("age", "Age (yr)") +
  check_linearity("pershrub", "Shrub cover (%)")
```

Bin each predictor, compute the empirical log-odds in each bin, and look
for a straight line. Shrub cover is close to one; with 25 fragments
these are rough.
:::
:::::

## Which Diagnostic for Which Family

::: {.compact-table}
| Family | What it assumes | What to check |
|------------|-----------------------------|---------------------------|
| **All GLMs** | Independence; correct link; no extreme leverage | DHARMa residuals, Cook's distance, VIF |
| **Gaussian** | Normal residuals, equal variance | `shapiro.test()`, Levene's, residual plots |
| **Poisson** | Counts; **variance = mean** | `check_overdispersion()`, `testDispersion()` |
| **Negative binomial** | Counts; variance = $\mu + \mu^2/\theta$ | `check_overdispersion()`, DHARMa |
| **Binomial / logistic** | Binary response; linear on the **logit** scale; enough events | Binned log-odds plot, Hosmer–Lemeshow, separation warnings |
:::

::: callout-important
**Check the diagnostic that matches the model you fitted**, not the one
you learned first. `shapiro.test()` on Poisson residuals will give you a
number, and the number will mean nothing.
:::

## Part 8 · GLMs, ANOVA, and Wrap-Up {.divider}

## One-Way ANOVA Is a Gaussian GLM {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
Every linear model you have fitted this semester is the special case of
a GLM where:

1.  The response is **normal**
2.  The link is the **identity**

So a one-way ANOVA, a linear regression on a categorical predictor, and
a Gaussian GLM are **three names for one fit**.

Here on **last week's crayfish** — a genuine two-level factor:

```{r glm-38}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
aov_fit <- aov(growth_per_day ~ range, data = cray_df)
lm_fit  <- lm(growth_per_day ~ range, data = cray_df)
glm_fit <- glm(growth_per_day ~ range, data = cray_df,
               family = gaussian(link = "identity"))
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r glm-39}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
round(cbind(aov = coef(aov_fit),
            lm  = coef(lm_fit),
            glm = coef(glm_fit)), 4)

c(aov = summary(aov_fit)[[1]][1, "F value"],
  lm  = anova(lm_fit)[1, "F value"])
```

::: callout-note
Identical coefficients, identical *F*. GLMs did not replace the ANOVA —
they contain it.
:::
:::
:::::

## Summary — What a GLM Gives You

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
1.  **Gaussian** + identity link = the linear model and ANOVA you
    already know
2.  **Poisson** + log link = counts — and always check the dispersion
3.  **Negative binomial** = counts whose variance exceeds the mean —
    common in ecology, but **check** rather than assume (the ants did
    not need it)
4.  **Binomial** + logit link = binary responses, read as odds ratios

What they share: the linear predictor is unchanged. You are still
fitting a straight line — just on a scale where a straight line cannot
predict something impossible.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: callout-important
**The method, not the models**

Fit it → check the diagnostic that matches the model → change one
assumption → refit.

Today that chain ran on one question and gave *p*-values from 10⁻¹⁹⁸ to
10⁻⁷, all of them tiny. The number was never the problem. What changed
was whether you were entitled to it.
:::

::: callout-note
**Up next — Linear Mixed Models**

The thing you change next week is not the distribution but the **error
structure**: random effects, and hierarchical designs done
properly.
:::
:::
:::::

## Summary — Choosing a Distribution and Link

1.  Look at the **response** first — is it continuous, a count, or a
    yes/no? That picks the family.
2.  Let the family pick the **link** unless you have a reason not to.
3.  Fit it, then run the diagnostic that belongs to **that** family.
4.  For counts, check overdispersion **every time**. It inflates
    significance and never warns you.
5.  Compare candidate families with **AIC** and with DHARMa residuals,
    not with whichever gives the smaller *p*.
6.  Report on the **response scale** — counts and probabilities, not log
    and logit — using `emmeans(type = "response")` or an odds ratio.

## Readings

::::::: columns
:::: {.column width="55%"}
- **Gotelli & Ellison**, Ch. 9 — Regression, for extending the linear model beyond ordinary least squares.
- **Gotelli & Ellison**, Ch. 11 — The Analysis of Categorical Data, for logistic regression and binomial GLMs.
- **Whitlock & Schluter**, Ch. 17 — Regression, §"Logistic regression", for the binary-response case.
- **Quinn & Keough** (2002), *Experimental Design and Data Analysis for Biologists*, Ch. 13 — Generalized Linear Models and Logistic Regression. This is the source of both worked examples today.
::::

:::: {.column width="45%"}
::: callout-note
**📖 On the datasets**

The *Uta* lizard data are Polis et al.'s, reproduced in Quinn & Keough **Box 13-1**. The canyon rodent data are Bolger et al.'s, reproduced in **Box 13-2**. The Galápagos and New England ant data are **Gotelli & Ellison**'s, from *A Primer of Ecological Statistics* (Ch. 8 and Ch. 9) — the Galápagos file is the same one you used in week 6.

The textbook PDFs are on Canvas.
:::

::: callout-tip
**🖐 Beyond the books**

Zuur et al. (2009), *Mixed Effects Models and Extensions in Ecology with R*, Ch. 9, is the standard ecological reference for overdispersion and the negative binomial.
:::
